title: I Capture the Castle
full_review:
An English girl learns bittersweet lessons about life and love in the tender coming-of-age tale, "I Capture the Castle" (Samuel Goldwyn).

In this film based on the Dodie Smith novel, director Tim Fywell elicits a strong performance out of his young lead, but the supporting ensemble is at times stilted, leaving much of the narrative scented with the mannered bouquet of a BBC melodrama.

Set in the 1930s and seen through the youthful eyes of 17-year-old Cassandra (Romola Garai) -- whose reflective diary musings supply the film's narration -- "I Capture the Castle" tells the story of the Mortmain family, an eccentric clan living in a dilapidated castle in the Suffolk countryside.

James Mortmain (Bill Nighy), the petulant patriarch, is a novelist haunted both by his past literary success and his emotional failings as a husband to his now-dead wife. Sharing the drafty keep with them is Rose (Rose Byrne), Cassandra's beautiful older sister, and younger brother Thomas (Joe Sowerbutts), as well as their bohemian stepmother, Topaz (Tara Fitzgerald), an avant-garde artist prone to stripping naked on the windswept moors.

Rounding out the quirky bunch of Brits is Stephen (Henry Cavill), a jack-of-all-trades, orphaned and left as a ward of the Mortmain household. Despite his chiseled good-looks, Stephen's infatuation with Cassandra is unrequited beyond sibling devotion.

The trouble starts when Mortmain, creatively impotent for the past 12 years, learns that his royalties -- the family's financial lifeline -- have dried up. On the heels of this blow they also receive the tragic news that their benevolent landlord, Sir William Cotton, by whose good grace they have been allowed to live in the castle, has died and that two years' back rent is now due.

With the unconventional -- but big-hearted -- Topaz at the helm, the family's loving kinship, good humor and irrepressible optimism allow them to weather the storm. However, their physical hardships pale in comparison with the emotional turmoil unleashed by the arrival of two Americans, Simon Cotton (Henry Thomas) and his brash younger brother, Neil (Marc Blucas), who have crossed the pond to claim their ancestral estate. They quickly take a shine to their kooky inherited tenants.

But while the sympathetic Yanks allay the Mortmains' fears over their growing debts, their dashing good looks also awaken new and exciting feelings of romance in Rose and Cassandra. Jealousy inevitably emerges as both Simon and Neil gravitate toward Rose.

What originally seemed like the answer to their prayers ultimately ends up testing the bonds of sisterhood. And though at one point she despairs, doubting the possibility of happiness, Cassandra closes on the hopeful affirmation, "I love, I have loved, I will love."

Imbued with a tremendous amount of hope, this modest fable poetically captures the difficult, sometimes painful, transition from childhood to becoming an adult. This maturing process is metaphorically communicated through juxtaposing the castle -- an archetypal image of childhood, full of enchanted gardens and bucolic redolence -- with the dinner clubs and boutiques of London's high society. These growing pains are mirrored eloquently in Garai's soulful eyes -- at once both probing and utterly vulnerable.

Another theme touched on is that of contrition. Each of the main characters both seeks and bestows forgiveness in varying degrees. This readiness to forgive -- best illustrated during a poignant scene shared by Cassandra and her father -- is the cement that keeps the family firm in their loving commitment to each other, as well as serving as the emotional engine that fuels much of the narrative.

This bond shared by the Mortmain family extends past the grave, with Cassandra's mother -- who appears only in brief flashbacks -- exerting, even in her physical absence, an inordinate influence, testifying to the profound mystery of love which lingers after earthly life fades.

Some Catholics may be put off by the Faustian pact Rose makes with a stone gargoyle, as well as the secret "pagan" rituals invented by the sisters in their youth. Both these scenes are meant more as narrative devices to visually convey the girl's lively imagination and almost childlike sense of primitive wonder than as any devotion to the occult.

Regrettably, the filmmaker chose to include a scene of Topaz standing nude with arms outstretched in a rainstorm, earning the film its R rating. While the actions were consistent with her off-kilter personality, it could have been handled in a more subtle and tasteful manner.

Due to brief frontal nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
